issues.subcategory: Farmer et al. measure in phonological-cue review
issues.description: Farmer et al. measure in phonological-cue review: The description of Farmer et al. (2006) appears to mix paradigms: a self-paced reading study would ordinarily yield reading-time measures, whereas “were read aloud faster” implies an overt naming or read-aloud latency. This makes it unclear whether the cited effect concerns self-paced reading times, naming latencies, or another dependent measure.
issues.quote: Language speakers extract these probabilistic cues from their environment, and exploit them in language learning and language processing. Cassidy and Kelly (1991, 2001) and Fitneva, Christiansen, and Monaghan (2009) found that children learn object and action referents better if there is a correspondence between the sounds of the nouns and verbs and their respective lexical categories. Further, using a self-paced reading methodology, Farmer et al. (2006) found that when sentence context generated an expectation for a noun, phonologically-typical nouns (e.g. marble whose phonological features cluster with those of other nouns) were read aloud faster than phonologically-atypical nouns (e.g. insect whose phonological features cluster with those of verbs). Information about lexical category is critical for comprehending language

issues.subcategory: Unclear exception logic in the -ED example
issues.description: Unclear exception logic in the -ED example: There seems to be an issue with the -ED example: the exception class is difficult to interpret because the passage describes the relevant words as morphologically simple while also saying they could be treated as comprising more than one morpheme. In addition, the examples do not all clearly instantiate the stated final sequence $/ \varepsilon \mathrm{d} /$. If the intended comparison is with the syllabic past-tense allomorph, the relevant final sequence is usually /ɪd/ or /əd/, especially for readers who pronounce “naked” and “wicked” with final /ɪd/ or /əd/. Meanwhile, “instead”, “biped”, and “moped” are more naturally /ɛd/ cases. This mixes distinct phonological endings and weakens the spelling-versus-sound comparison in this illustrative paragraph.
issues.quote:
Similar dependency characterizes English inflectional suffixes. For example, it is well known that spelling -ED is
strongly indicative of past tense (e.g. Carney, 1994). However, it has only recently come to light that the word-final sound sequence $/ \varepsilon \mathrm{d} /$ in morphologically-simple words is typically spelled in a different manner (e.g. instead; Berg et al., 2014). In fact, there are only a handful of morphologically-simple words ending in this sound sequence spelled -ED that could potentially be treated as comprising more than one morpheme (e.g. biped, moped, naked, wicked; Berg et al., 2014).

issues.subcategory: Analogy between writing and speech runs in the wrong direction
issues.description: Analogy between writing and speech runs in the wrong direction: The -ED example is being used to argue that writing preserves a form–meaning distinction better than speech does. Intonation and emphasis are the opposite kind of case: speech preserves information that ordinary writing often loses. Replace “just like” with “in contrast to” or recast the sentence, otherwise the analogy briefly points away from the argument that follows.
issues.quote: Thus, the relationship between form and meaning in this instance appears to be stronger in written language than in spoken language - just like other types of meaningful information are preserved in speech, but lost in writing (e.g. intonation, emphasis; Seidenberg, 2017).

issues.subcategory: Erroneous phonetic notation for the -OUS example
issues.description: Erroneous phonetic notation for the -OUS example: The phonological transcription for the -OUS example appears erroneous: the passage gives $/ \partial \mathrm{S} /$, whereas the surrounding text uses /-əs/. Because this sentence introduces specificity, the notation risks obscuring the intended comparison among words ending in the same spoken sequence.
issues.quote: Thus, if we apply these new constructs to the linguistic analysis of Berg and Aronoff (2017), we see that the written suffix -OUS is both highly diagnostic (its written form cues the adjective meaning) and highly specific for adjectives if a word ends in the sound sequence $/ \partial \mathrm{S} /$. In this case, the written suffix -OUS appears to be reserved for adjectives, as opposed to other categories of words that end in the same sequence of sounds (meaning dictates the spelling).

issues.subcategory: Specificity definition drops the sound-sequence condition
issues.description: Specificity definition drops the sound-sequence condition: The parenthetical description is too loose for the construct introduced in this section. Specificity is not simply P(cue | category); it is conditioned on a shared final sound sequence, for example P(-OUS | adjective, /-əs/). Without that sound condition, the denominator changes from adjectives with the relevant pronunciation to all adjectives, which is a different quantity. Please revise the parenthesis to something like “probability of a cue given a category and a sound sequence”.
issues.quote: Here we hypothesise that the bidirectional relationship between the form and the meaning cannot be captured using a unitary concept (e.g. cue validity), and needs to be expressed through the combination of diagnosticity and specificity (probability of a cue given a category).

issues.subcategory: Token specificity denominator in Method
issues.description: Token specificity denominator in Method: The token-based specificity definition appears to use the wrong denominator. Specificity is defined relative to all spellings of a given word-final sound sequence within a lexical category, but the token formula says to divide by the summed frequency of words that contain the target spelling and fall in that category. That denominator would condition on the spelling rather than on the sound sequence, so it is not the token analogue of the preceding type-based measure.
issues.quote: We define specificity as the extent to which a suffix spelling is preferred for denoting a particular lexical category, amongst all possible spellings of a sound sequence. In order to calculate specificity, we identified the most frequent pronunciation of each suffix, and then extracted all words from our single-word database containing that word-final sound sequence. Note that CELEX lists surface phonological forms (not phonetic/allophonic forms). We stayed as close to the CELEX forms as we could to avoid theoretical controversies. For example, the sound sequence /ləs/ associated with suffix -LESS also occurs in words with other word-final spellings (e.g. necklace, malice). For a given lexical category, we then divided the number of words containing the suffix spelling (e.g. -LESS) by the total number of words of this lexical category with any spelling of the sound sequence. Like diagnosticity, specificity is expressed as a ratio ranging from 0 to 1 . Spellings with the specificity of 0 for a given category never go with this category (e.g. -IOUS never occurs in nouns), whereas the value of 1 indicates that the spelling has full specificity (e.g. when a noun ends in /ertə/, it must be spelled with -ATOR). Medium values of specificity indicate that there are multiple competing spellings, as with /ɪə/ (specificity of 0.48 , cf. cashier, engineer). A second measure of specificity, based on word tokens, was obtained by dividing the summed frequency of words ending in this phonological and orthographic sequence and falling into this category by the summed frequency of all words that contain the spelling and fall into this category.

issues.subcategory: Mathematical contradiction in Specificity metric
issues.description: Mathematical contradiction in Specificity metric: There seems to be an issue with the stated denominator for specificity: values of 1.000 for suffixes such as +ate and +ment are hard to reconcile with the description as “all” words in a lexical category sharing the relevant final sound sequence. If the denominator was restricted to candidate suffixed or pseudo-suffixed forms under the stem constraint, that restriction is important for interpreting the metric.
issues.quote: For a given lexical category, we then divided the number of words containing the suffix spelling (e.g. -LESS) by the total number of words of this lexical category with any spelling of the sound sequence. Like diagnosticity, specificity is expressed as a ratio ranging from 0 to 1 .

issues.subcategory: Suffix-level values not fully specified in Results
issues.description: Suffix-level values not fully specified in Results: The suffix-level aggregation used for Figure 2, the means, and the correlations is not fully specified. The Method and Appendix define diagnosticity and specificity separately for noun, adjective, and verb values, but the Results report one diagnosticity and one specificity value per suffix. It is therefore unclear whether these values are maxima, dominant-category values, averages, or something else.
issues.quote:
Figure 2 plot diagnosticity and specificity values for English derivational suffixes. The majority of suffixes are either
diagnostic or specific or both. Mean type diagnosticity for suffixes is 0.78 (token -0.77 ), mean specificity is 0.82 (token0.83 ). The correlation between the type variables is $0.53, \mathrm{p}<0.0001$; that between the token variables $-0.47, \mathrm{p}<$ 0.0001 . This indicates that the two constructs are related although they capture distinct properties of suffixes. The full range of diagnosticity and specificity values are contained in Appendix A.

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent suffix counts in Results
issues.description: Inconsistent suffix counts in Results: The robustness-check counts are internally inconsistent: the computational analysis reports 154 written suffixes, but this passage says 64 suffixes were excluded and 95 remained. Those numbers cannot all be correct, so the exclusion count, retained count, or sampling frame for the frequency-threshold analysis needs clarification.
issues.quote: It is immediately apparent that a substantial number of suffixes have diagnosticity and specificity values of 1 . This means that these suffix spellings are always associated with a particular lexical category (diagnosticity) and that these suffix spellings are the only means of communicating a particular lexical category for a given word-final sound sequence (specificity). Is it possible that this very strong relationship between spelling and lexical category is due to the presence of suffixes in our sample that occur only rarely? In order to determine this, we excluded all suffixes that occur in fewer than 20 different words in the CELEX database, i.e. 64 suffixes (Baayen et al., 1993). For the remaining 95 suffixes, the mean diagnosticity and specificity values were virtually unchanged (type and token diagnosticity mean $=0.76$; type specificity mean $=0.83$, token specificity mean $=0.82$ ).

issues.subcategory: Rarity check does not test whether exact-one values remain
issues.description: Rarity check does not test whether exact-one values remain: The paragraph motivates the exclusion by pointing to the many suffixes with diagnosticity or specificity exactly equal to 1, but the check reports only post-exclusion means. Those means can remain high even if the exact-one cases mostly disappear. Add counts among the retained suffixes: how many have diagnosticity = 1, how many have specificity = 1, and how many have both. That would answer the question the paragraph sets up.
issues.quote: For the remaining 95 suffixes, the mean diagnosticity and specificity values were virtually unchanged (type and token diagnosticity mean $=0.76$; type specificity mean $=0.83$, token specificity mean $=0.82$ ).

issues.subcategory: Conclusion shifts from a union claim to an intersection claim
issues.description: Conclusion shifts from a union claim to an intersection claim: As written, this says that most suffixes satisfy both properties at once. The Results section supports the weaker statement that most suffixes are diagnostic, specific, or both. Those are not equivalent: a large union does not imply a large intersection. If the intended claim is that a majority have both high diagnosticity and high specificity, report the intersection count and the threshold used. Otherwise, soften the sentence to “diagnostic, specific, or both”.
issues.quote: Our analyses demonstrate that the majority of written English derivational suffixes are diagnostic and specific for some lexical category.

issues.subcategory: Incomplete random effects structure in mixed model
issues.description: Incomplete random effects structure in mixed model: The Experiment 1 mixed model may have an overly sparse random-effects structure. Because suffix condition is manipulated within participants, a by-subject random slope for condition would usually be considered; and because the same 80 nonword stems/items appear to contribute repeated observations across participants and are nested under suffixes, an item or stem random intercept may also be needed in addition to the suffix intercept. Without some justification or robustness check showing that the reported suffix-condition and diagnosticity effects are robust to item/stem variation, the reported standard error for the fixed effect of condition may be anti-conservative.
issues.quote: We included two random intercepts, one for subjects and one for suffixes. This analysis was expressed in the model glmer (response $\sim$ condition $+(1 \mid$ subject $)+(1 \mid$ suffix $)$, data, family $=$ "binomial").

issues.subcategory: Experiment 1 coefficient is used for a within-condition claim
issues.description: Experiment 1 coefficient is used for a within-condition claim: The reported coefficient tests the contrast between adjective- and noun-diagnostic suffix conditions. It does not, on its own, test whether noun-diagnostic suffixes received more noun than adjective responses within that condition; that requires the intercept and coding, or model-predicted probabilities with intervals. Rephrase this as a between-condition effect, or add the within-condition predicted probabilities if that is the claim you want readers to take from the result.
issues.quote: Results showed a main effect of suffix condition such that noun-diagnostic suffixes elicited more "noun" responses ( $\mathrm{B}=-1.57, \mathrm{z}=-4.224, \mathrm{p}<0.0001$ ) than "adjective" responses.

issues.subcategory: Signed diagnosticity predictor is interpreted as diagnosticity magnitude
issues.description: Signed diagnosticity predictor is interpreted as diagnosticity magnitude: The signed predictor mixes category direction with diagnosticity strength. For adjective suffixes, larger diagnosticity gives a larger predictor value; for noun suffixes, larger diagnosticity gives a more negative value. The combined coefficient therefore shows that a signed category score predicts adjective versus noun responses. It is not, by itself, a clean test that stronger diagnosticity within a category produces more category-consistent decisions. The category-specific analyses that follow are the right place to make that graded claim, so the summary sentence should be revised accordingly.
issues.quote: In order to investigate this statistically, we multiplied our diagnosticity measure by -1 for noun-diagnostic suffixes and substituted this measure in our model, in place of the condition variable. This analysis revealed a main effect of diagnosticity on response type: $\mathrm{B}=0.87, \mathrm{z}=4.13$, $\mathrm{p}<0.0001$, such that more diagnostic suffixes were more likely to be ascribed to the category that they denote.

issues.subcategory: Diagnosticity and specificity blur in Experiment 1
issues.description: Diagnosticity and specificity blur in Experiment 1: In Experiment 1, “adjective-specific suffixes” appears to be a terminological slip: the analysis is explicitly of diagnosticity and is contrasted with “noun-diagnostic suffixes”. Because specificity is a separate construct used for Experiment 2, this wording could blur the intended distinction between diagnosticity and specificity.
issues.quote:
We performed this analysis separately for adjective- and noun- diagnostic suffixes to make sure that this effect was not due
to the sign-transformation of the diagnosticity variable, and observed the effect of diagnosticity on both adjective-specific suffixes ( $B=4.5, z=2.9, p<0.01$, i.e. highest absolute values for diagnosticity yield more adjective responses) and noun-diagnostic suffixes ( $B=-3.5, z=-2.05, p<0.05$, i.e. highest absolute values for diagnosticity yield more noun responses; see Figure 4). The results based on token measures were similar (main effect of diagnosticity, and an effect of diagnosticity on noun-diagnostic suffixes), but adjective-specific suffixes did not show an effect of diagnosticity ( $p>$ 0.8).

issues.subcategory: Spurious parametric effect driven by outliers
issues.description: Spurious parametric effect driven by outliers: The within-category diagnosticity effects in Experiment 1 may be driven disproportionately by the lowest-diagnosticity suffixes, especially +an among noun suffixes and +y among adjective suffixes. Most other diagnosticity values in Table 2 are clustered near the top of the scale, so the evidence for a fine-grained parametric effect within each category is less secure without showing that the slopes are not mainly leverage effects from those suffixes.
issues.quote: and observed the effect of diagnosticity on both adjective-specific suffixes ( $B=4.5, z=2.9, p<0.01$, i.e. highest absolute values for diagnosticity yield more adjective responses) and noun-diagnostic suffixes ( $B=-3.5, z=-2.05, p<0.05$, i.e. highest absolute values for diagnosticity yield more noun responses; see Figure 4).

issues.subcategory: Item-level control is unclear in Experiment 2
issues.description: Item-level control is unclear in Experiment 2: The control argument in Experiment 2 seems too broad. Reusing the same suffix pronunciation across congruent and incongruent contexts controls the spoken ending and alternative suffix spellings, but the congruent and incongruent trials appear to use different stems and sentence frames, with no reported item-level random effect or counterbalancing of nonword/sentence items across condition. This leaves open item- or frame-level sources of variation in suffix spelling choices.
issues.quote: Stimuli. Eleven suffix spellings that had a high specificity for noun, adjective, or verb lexical category were selected. These were considered as the target spellings. Critically, the pronunciation most frequently associated with these suffixes could be spelled in more than one way (see Table 3). Note that no matching was required, because the same phonological sequence was used in the congruent and incongruent conditions. Thus, any effect could not be attributed to the properties of the phonological sequence or its possible spellings: for instance, had it been the spelling frequency that influenced participants' performance, we would observe no difference between the conditions at all (i.e., the most frequent spelling would be used regardless of the predicted lexical category).

issues.subcategory: Target-versus-other spelling does not show category-specific alternatives
issues.description: Target-versus-other spelling does not show category-specific alternatives: The binary coding of “target spelling” versus “other spelling” can show that participants used -OUS less often in noun contexts. It does not show that the spellings they produced in those contexts were noun-diagnostic; “other” could include phonetic spellings or idiosyncratic choices with no noun link. Either code the alternative spellings by their category associations, or state the inference more narrowly as suppression of the target spelling outside its congruent category.
issues.quote: For instance, three different /əs/-nonwords were embedded in sentences where they functioned as adjectives (congruent context where the target spelling -OUS is expected), and three different/əs/-nonwords were embedded in sentences where they functioned as nouns (any other spelling is expected but not-OUS).

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent token-analysis statistic in Experiment 2
issues.description: Inconsistent token-analysis statistic in Experiment 2: The token-analysis statistic in Experiment 2 is internally inconsistent: $z=0.60$ or $z=-0.60$ cannot yield $p<0.01$ under the Wald-test reporting convention used elsewhere in the paper. The paper needs to make clear whether the token-based specificity interaction was significant, or whether the $z$ or $p$ value was misreported.
issues.quote: Further analyses were conducted to investigate whether participants' knowledge of suffix specificity for lexical category mirrors statistics of the writing system. In other words, is the effect of condition (congruent vs incongruent) larger for suffixes whose spelling is highly specific for lexical category than for those with a weaker specificity? In order to investigate this hypothesis, we added the graded specificity metric for the target spelling to the linear model (values were different in different contexts because specificity of spellings was estimated relative to different categories), as well as its interaction with the condition variable. As predicted, the interaction between specificity and condition was significant, such that the target spelling became used more often in the congruent condition than in the incongruent condition as its specificity increased ( $B=1.9, z=2.8, p<0.01$; for the token analyses $-z=0.60, p<0.01$ ); there was no effect of specificity in the incongruent condition.

issues.subcategory: Context-dependent specificity changes the tested interaction
issues.description: Context-dependent specificity changes the tested interaction: The preceding question asks whether the congruent–incongruent difference is larger for suffixes whose target spelling has higher specificity. If the specificity value changes between the two condition rows for the same suffix, the interaction term is no longer that simple within-suffix moderation. With treatment coding, the condition contrast includes both the condition-by-specificity term and the change from S_congruent to S_incongruent. Furthermore, Table 3 reports a single specificity value for each target spelling, which makes the construction of the specificity predictor not fully transparent. Either use one target-category specificity value per suffix in both conditions, or restate the model as testing context-specific specificity, report the implied condition contrasts directly, and clarify if any context-specific specificity values were undefined.
issues.quote: In order to investigate this hypothesis, we added the graded specificity metric for the target spelling to the linear model (values were different in different contexts because specificity of spellings was estimated relative to different categories), as well as its interaction with the condition variable.

issues.subcategory: Experiment 2 discussion should say spoken nonwords
issues.description: Experiment 2 discussion should say spoken nonwords: Experiment 2 used spoken nonwords, not existing spoken words. That distinction matters because existing words bring word-specific spellings into play, while the experiment tests generalisation to novel forms. A more accurate sentence would be: “when presented with a spoken nonword in a sentence context, participants were more likely to produce spellings appropriate for the predicted lexical category.”
issues.quote: Thus, when presented with a spoken word in a sentence context, they produce spellings that are appropriate for the predicted lexical category.

issues.subcategory: Verb filler status is contradictory in Experiment 3 stimuli
issues.description: Verb filler status is contradictory in Experiment 3 stimuli: The description of the Experiment 3 fillers appears internally inconsistent. The filler nonwords are described as having verb-diagnostic suffix spellings, but the next sentence says verb suffixes generally have diagnosticity below 0.5, and Appendix A indicates that most of the listed filler suffixes are not verb-diagnostic by the paper's own metric. This makes the intended role of the verb fillers ambiguous, even though they were not analysed. A cleaner description would be “verb-associated suffix spellings” or “suffix spellings used in verb frames”, followed by the explanation that they were fillers and not analysed as diagnostic verb cues.
issues.quote: Stimuli. Eighty experimental nonwords with suffix spellings diagnostic for adjectives ( 10 suffixes) or nouns ( 10 suffixes) were selected from Experiment 1. Forty filler nonwords whose suffix spellings were diagnostic for verbs were added so that sentence contexts would be more varied. These filler nonwords were not analysed, because the majority of verb suffixes do not discriminate lexical category (i.e. diagnosticity is less than 0.5 ). The ten verb suffixes we used as fillers were -ate, -ade, -eer, -le, -yse, -ide, -our, -ice, -ure, -art. Orthographic neighbourhood size for experimental nonwords ranged between 0 and 4 , mean 0.45 , median 0 .

issues.subcategory: Incorrect degrees of freedom for stimulus matching
issues.description: Incorrect degrees of freedom for stimulus matching: The reported degrees of freedom for the pre-target word-count comparison are difficult to interpret from the design description. If the comparison used 40 congruent and 40 incongruent analysed items, an equal-variance item test would have 78 df; all 120 sentences would imply a different basis. The $\mathrm{t}(64)$ value may be legitimate if it comes from a Welch test or a particular subset, but that basis is not evident here.
issues.quote: Sentence parts preceding targets were matched across conditions on the number of letters (congruent: 30.48 letters on average, incongruent: 31.70 letters, $p>0.3$ ). Note that the number of words pre-target was slightly different across conditions (congruent: 4.75, incongruent: 5.23, $\mathrm{t}(64)=2.07, \mathrm{p}<0.05$ ).

issues.subcategory: Pre-target word length appears to refer to the immediately preceding word
issues.description: Pre-target word length appears to refer to the immediately preceding word: The wording suggests all words before the target, but the numbers do not fit that reading. The earlier totals give 30.48 letters / 4.75 words = 6.42 letters per word in the congruent condition and 31.70 / 5.23 = 6.06 in the incongruent condition, not 7.33 and 7.15. These values seem to describe the word immediately before the target. Say that directly, since that is the unit relevant for launch-site control and skipping.
issues.quote: Pretarget words were always at least five characters long (with no difference across conditions: $7.33 \mathrm{vs} 7.15, \mathrm{p}>0.6$ ), to reduce the likelihood of these words being skipped.

issues.subcategory: Comprehension accuracy is reported with the wrong unit
issues.description: Comprehension accuracy is reported with the wrong unit: As written, 0.86% means 0.0086 as a proportion, which would be fewer than one correct answer per 100 comprehension questions. The intended values appear to be proportions or percentages, but the current units misstate an important data-quality check for the eye-tracking experiment. Report them as either “0.86 (range 0.66–0.98)” or “86% (range 66%–98%)”.
issues.quote: Average accuracy on comprehension trials was $0.86 \%$ (ranging from $0.66 \%$ to $0.98 \%$ ).

issues.subcategory: Mismatch in Experiment 3 statistics
issues.description: Mismatch in Experiment 3 statistics: The Experiment 3 Results text and Table 5 report different model values for the same congruency effects. The text gives go-past time as $B=41$, $t=3.837$ and regressions-out as $B=0.3$, $z=3.12$, whereas Table 5 gives go-past time as $B=43$, $t=3.76$ and regressions-out as $B=0.25$, $z=2.65$. The significance pattern is unchanged, but the values should be reconciled.
issues.quote:
There was an effect of congruency on go-past time ( $\mathrm{B}=41, \mathrm{t}=3.837, \mathrm{p}<0.001$ ) such that go-past times were longer for incongruent trials than for congruent ones.

Regressions-in. This analysis considered the impact of congruency on whether the target received at least one regression from later parts of the sentence. $34 \%$ of all trials available for analysis contained such regressions. There was no effect of congruency on this measure.

Regressions-out. This analysis considered the impact of congruency on whether regression(s) were made from the target to previous parts of the sentence prior to leaving in a forward direction. $15 \%$ of all trials available for analysis contained such regressions. The effect of congruency on regressions-out was significant in the expected direction, i.e. incongruent targets were more likely to elicit regressions to earlier regions of the sentence ( $B=0.3, z=3.12, p<0.01$ ).

issues.subcategory: Regressions-in are grouped with initial-processing measures
issues.description: Regressions-in are grouped with initial-processing measures: The non-significant measures include regressions-in, which the paper defines as returns to the target from later parts of the sentence. That is a later reinspection measure, not an initial lexical-processing measure in the same sense as skipping, first fixation duration, or first-run dwell time. Separate the interpretation: early measures showed no congruency effect, regressions-in also showed no effect, and the clearest effects appeared in go-past time and regressions-out.
issues.quote: We did not find any significant effect of congruency on any of the other measures reported, all of which are thought to reflect initial lexical processing (e.g. Rayner \& Liversedge, 2011).

issues.subcategory: Degrees of freedom mismatch (Results)
issues.description: Degrees of freedom mismatch (Results): There seems to be an issue with the regressions-out model comparison: the text says model fit improved when the interaction was added, but the likelihood-ratio test is reported with 2 degrees of freedom. For a binary congruency factor and continuous diagnosticity predictor, adding only the interaction would normally add 1 parameter; the reported degrees of freedom suggest that the diagnosticity main effect may also have been added, or that the degrees of freedom are misstated.
issues.quote: The fit of regressions-out model improved significantly when the interaction was added: Chi $(2)=14.37, \mathrm{p}<0.001$. The original model produced a convergence warning when the variables were added.

issues.subcategory: Simple slopes are described as a main effect
issues.description: Simple slopes are described as a main effect: These are conditional slopes under a diagnosticity-by-congruency interaction, not a single main effect. If congruent trials are the reference condition, the diagnosticity slope in congruent trials is βD = -0.15, while the incongruent slope is βD + βDC, which matches the reported positive value after rounding. The reported B=0.37 term is the interaction or slope contrast. Please call these “simple slopes” or “condition-specific effects” so the model interpretation matches the coefficients.
issues.quote: First, there was a main effect of diagnosticity: the probability of regressing to previous regions of the sentence decreased as diagnosticity increased in the congruent condition ( $\mathrm{B}=-0.15, \mathrm{z}=-2.31, \mathrm{p}<0.05$ ), and increased as diagnosticity increased in the incongruent condition (marginal significance, $\mathrm{B}=0.21, \mathrm{z}=1.8, \mathrm{p}=0.08$ ).

issues.subcategory: Discussion seems to reverse the orthographic premise
issues.description: Discussion seems to reverse the orthographic premise: The opening of the Discussion could be read as understating English orthographic depth: saying that letters map ‘relatively consistently’ to sounds sits uneasily with the later claim that English has a highly inconsistent spelling-sound mapping, unless the intended comparison is only with non-alphabetic writing systems.
issues.quote: English has an alphabetic writing system in which letters map relatively consistently to sounds. However, it is well known that additional regularities between spelling and meaning arise as a result of morphological relationships between words. Stems occur repeatedly in words of similar meanings (e.g. builder, building, rebuild) and affixes alter the meanings of words in predictable ways (e.g. teacher, builder, banker; Rastle et al., 2000). A wide variety of research suggests that skilled readers acquire knowledge of these regularities, and use this knowledge in the recognition of words (e.g. Rastle \& Davis, 2008; Taft \& Forster, 1975).

issues.subcategory: Learning claim goes beyond the behavioural evidence
issues.description: Learning claim goes beyond the behavioural evidence: The claim that the paper has shown that the average reader learns these cues without explicit instruction appears to go beyond the direct behavioural evidence. The experiments show that skilled adult readers are sensitive to, and use, suffix-based lexical-category cues, but the learning process and participants’ instructional histories are inferred rather than tested.
issues.quote: The acquisition of skilled reading involves the accumulation of years of experience with the writing system. In light of the large proportion of the English lexicon characterised by derivational suffixation, we hypothesized that these regularities might be encoded in the long-term knowledge of skilled readers. Results of these investigations were unambiguous. Across three experiments using different paradigms, we found that these regularities impacted on the reading, spelling, and decision-making behaviour of skilled readers. We have shown that the average reader learns and subsequently relies on morphological cues to class even without explicit instruction to do so (see our spelling and eye tracking data) suggesting that these cues facilitate access to meaning.

issues.subcategory: Entropy category set is unclear after earlier restrictions
issues.description: Entropy category set is unclear after earlier restrictions: The entropy calculation does not clearly state which lexical-category inventory is used for the summation. Earlier analyses foreground nouns, adjectives, and verbs, but Appendix A reports some entropy values above $\log_2(3)$, which would be impossible if $H$ were computed only over those three categories. This affects interpretation of the spelling–phonology entropy comparison because entropy depends directly on the category set over which uncertainty is measured.
issues.quote: In order to quantify the extent to which English suffix spellings convey more information about lexical category than English sound sequences, we analysed each suffix in terms of the entropy of its spelling and phonological realisation. Entropy (H) is an information-theoretic measure of uncertainty (Shannon, 1948), which has previously been used to quantify the relationship between spelling and sound (e.g. Mousikou, Sadat, Lucas, \& Rastle, 2017). We can calculate the entropy of each suffix spelling / spoken realisation using the formula $\Sigma[-\mathrm{pi} \times \log 2(\mathrm{pi})]$, where pi is the proportion of words belonging to a given lexical category. H values of 0 denote that the ending occurs in words of only one category

issues.subcategory: Entropy regression: slope is over-interpreted
issues.description: Entropy regression: slope is over-interpreted: In the entropy comparison, the slope from $\operatorname{lm}(H_{\mathrm{spelling}} \sim H_{\mathrm{phonology}})$ is over-interpreted. Because the model includes an intercept by default, a slope of 1 is not the identity line, and a slope below 1 does not by itself show that $H_{\mathrm{spelling}} < H_{\mathrm{phonology}}$ overall. The stated conclusion should instead be tied to a direct paired or weighted comparison of the entropies, or to an analysis of the fitted line relative to the identity line that includes the intercept.
